sections.h: The life is in the blood
sections.b: Leviticus 17 gives the Bible's fullest reason for the blood ban: "a body's life is in its blood, and I myself have given it to you on the altar, to make atonement for your lives" (17:11). Every ox, sheep or goat killed in the camp was to be brought to the tent as a peace offering, so that its blood went on the altar (17:3–6). Hunters must pour out the blood of game and cover it with dirt (17:13). The ban binds the foreigner as well as the Israelite (17:10, 12), which is one reason scholars link it with the rules for Gentile believers in Acts 15:20, 29. Jewish kosher slaughter, soaking and salting all aim to remove blood, and covering the blood of game is still done with a blessing.

common: Blood stands for life, and life belongs to God, so it may be offered but not eaten.
uncommon: Jehovah's Witnesses apply the blood ban of Leviticus 17 and Acts 15 to blood transfusions.

sections.b: Leviticus forbids handing children over "to make them pass over to Molech" (18:21) and sets death by stoning for it; if the people look away, God himself will cut off the man and his clan (20:2–5). The Samaritan Pentateuch reads "make serve" and the Septuagint "serve a ruler." Readers divide on three questions. Was Molech a god (John Day, George Heider) or a kind of offering (Otto Eissfeldt)? Were children killed, as Jeremiah 7:31, Ezekiel 16:20–21, Ezekiel 23:37–39 and Psalm 106:37–38 say of the rites in their day (Morton Smith), or dedicated by passing through fire, as the rabbis held (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:7; Talmud, Sanhedrin 64b; Maimonides) along with Norman Snaith and Moshe Weinfeld? And was it a foreign cult or one some Israelites thought the LORD accepted? The infant urns at Carthage's tophet are read by most as sacrifice (Stager and Wolff) and by some as a children's cemetery. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan reads 18:21 as fathering children with a Gentile woman for foreign worship.
sections.refs: Leviticus 18:21; Leviticus 20:1–5; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 32:35; Ezekiel 16:20–21; Psalm 106:37–38

common: Molech worship involved burning children, which the Bible condemns as the worst of idolatry.
Rabbinic tradition and some modern scholars read "passing over" to Molech as a dedication by fire that did not kill the child.
uncommon: Otto Eissfeldt and his followers hold that Molech was not a god at all but the name of a kind of offering.

sections.b: The Holiness Code says, "With a male do not lie down in the ways of lying down with a woman. It is abhorrent" (18:22), and sets death for both men (20:13). The phrase "lyings of a woman" is unusual, and much of the debate turns on it. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take it as an absolute ban on male–male intercourse, binding on all people. Jacob Milgrom read it as limited to anal intercourse and to Israelites and residents of the land. Saul Olyan argued that 18:22 first addressed only the active partner. James Brownson argues that the setting of such laws differs from modern committed partnerships; Robert Gagnon answers that the law's form is absolute and its basis is creation; revisionists reply that the New Testament also repeated the blood ban (Acts 15:20), which most churches set aside. The verses' Greek wording seems to lie behind Paul's word arsenokoitai (1 Corinthians 6:9).

common: Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 forbid sex between men, and Christians and Jews have traditionally applied this to all people.
uncommon: Some scholars hold that the verses address only Israelite men in the land, or only specific acts, and do not speak to modern committed relationships.

sections.b: "Do not take vengeance, and do not keep a grudge against the children of your people. You are to love your neighbor as yourself" (19:18). The command comes at the end of a list about the deaf and the blind, fair judging, slander and hidden hatred (19:14–17), so love here is action as well as feeling. The Sifra and Ramban read verses 17 and 18 together: honest correction, rather than silent resentment, is itself a form of love (see also James Kugel, 1987). Sixteen verses later the same words reach the outsider: "The foreigner who lives with you is to be to you like one born among you. You are to love him as yourself, because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" (19:34). Rabbi Akiva called 19:18 a great principle of the Torah; Jesus, Paul and James quote it as the summary of the law.

common: "Love your neighbor as yourself" is the moral heart of both the Old and New Testaments.
uncommon: Some read "as yourself" as "love your neighbor, who is a person like you," a call to see the other as equal rather than a measure of self-love.

sections.b: Leviticus 20 names death for Molech worship, mediums, cursing parents, adultery, several kinds of incest, male–male intercourse and bestiality, and chapter 24 adds blasphemy and murder. The phrase "their blood is on them" puts the guilt on the offender, not the community. The rabbis set strict rules of evidence and debated how often a court should ever execute (see the note on Leviticus 20:27). Christian tradition, from Aquinas to the Westminster Confession, treats these penalties as part of Israel's civil law that ended with its state, though some Puritans and modern theonomists sought to revive them.

common: The Mosaic death penalties belonged to Israel's civil law and do not bind modern states.
uncommon: Christian theonomists argue that civil governments today should enforce the penalties of the law of Moses.

sections.b: Leviticus 23 is the Torah's fullest list of "the LORD's set times." It begins with the weekly Sabbath (23:3) and runs through the year: Passover and Unleavened Bread (23:5–8), the first sheaf (23:9–14), the Feast of Weeks fifty days later (23:15–21), the day of trumpet blasts (23:23–25), the Day of Atonement (23:26–32) and the Feast of Booths (23:33–43). Each "holy gathering" stops ordinary work. The disputed phrase "the day after the Sabbath" (23:11, 15) divided Pharisees, Sadducees and later Karaites over when to count to Weeks. A reminder to leave the field's edges for the poor stands in the middle of the list (23:22).

common: Christians widely read the spring feasts as fulfilled in Jesus' death, resurrection and the gift of the Spirit.
uncommon: Some Christians hold that the fall feasts foretell the order of events at Christ's return: trumpets, judgment and God dwelling with his people.

sections.b: Leviticus 23:33–43 sets the Feast of Booths from the fifteenth of the seventh month, for seven days, with a closing assembly on the eighth. On the first day the people take "the fruit of beautiful trees, palm fronds, branches of thick-leaved trees and poplars of the valley stream" and rejoice before the LORD (23:40). Jewish tradition takes these as the four species waved at Sukkot (see the note on Leviticus 23:40). Everyone born in Israel is to live in booths, "so that your descendants will know that I made the Israelites live in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt" (23:43).

common: The booths remember Israel's tents in the wilderness and God's care for them there.
uncommon: Rabbi Eliezer held that the "booths" of 23:43 were the clouds of glory that surrounded Israel, not real huts (Talmud, Sukkah 11b).

sections.b: Leviticus ends with rules for paying vows. A person vowed to God is redeemed by a fixed value: fifty shekels for a man aged twenty to sixty, thirty for a woman, less for children and the old, and what a poor man can afford (27:1–8). An animal fit for sacrifice once vowed is holy and may not be swapped (27:9–10); an unfit animal, house or field can be redeemed with a fifth added (27:11–25). Firstborn animals and anything "devoted" cannot be vowed, since they already belong to God (27:26–29). Leviticus 22:17–25 adds that vowed animals must be without defect.

common: Vows to God are voluntary, but once made they must be kept.
uncommon: A midrash says Jephthah could have redeemed his daughter by the values of Leviticus 27 (Genesis Rabbah 60:3).

sections.b: Leviticus 25 sets a Sabbath year every seventh year, when the land is not sown and its produce is for all (25:1–7), and the Jubilee in the fiftieth year, announced with the ram's horn on the Day of Atonement (25:8–12). In the Jubilee each family returns to its land, because "the land is mine" (25:23), and Israelites who sold themselves as debt servants go free, because "they are my servants" (25:42). Land prices follow the years left to the Jubilee (25:14–17). God promises that the sixth year will produce enough for three (25:20–22). Leviticus 26:34–35 warns that if Israel does not give the land its Sabbaths, exile will.

No biblical narrative records a Jubilee. The rabbis said it lapsed with the exile of the eastern tribes (Talmud, Arakhin 32b). Many scholars see it as a reform of ancient royal debt releases (Moshe Weinfeld), others as a priestly ideal never put into effect. The Sabbath year, by contrast, is attested in Nehemiah 10:31, 1 Maccabees 6:49–53 and Josephus, and is kept in Israel today.

common: The Jubilee teaches that land and people belong to God, and that poverty must not become permanent.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Jubilee was never practiced at all and was written as a critique of the land policies of Israel's kings.

sections.b: Leviticus 26 builds through stages of warning to its climax: "you I will scatter among the nations" (26:33). The cities will be ruins, the sanctuaries desolate, and the survivors will flee at the sound of a leaf (26:31–36). Then "the land will make up for its Sabbaths" (26:34), a verse 2 Chronicles 36:21 applies to the Babylonian exile. Yet the chapter ends in hope: when the people confess and their "uncircumcised heart" is humbled, God will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, and "I will not reject them" (26:40–45). Critical scholars often date this section to the exile; traditional readers see it as prophecy.

common: Leviticus 26 foretells the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles and the return.
uncommon: Some scholars read Leviticus 26:34–43 as written after the exile, explaining it as the land's long-delayed Sabbath rest.

sections.b: Chapters 17–26 are called the Holiness Code because of their refrain: "You will be holy, because I am holy, I the LORD your God" (19:2; 20:26; compare 11:44). In chapters 1–16 holiness belongs mainly to the sanctuary and priests; here it reaches the whole people and the whole of life: the family (18; 20), the field and the market (19:9–10, 35–36), the courts (19:15), the calendar (23) and the land itself (25). God is "the LORD who makes you holy" (20:8; 21:8; 22:32), so holiness is both his gift and Israel's task. Israel Knohl and Jacob Milgrom see this as the work of a distinct priestly school, H.

common: Holiness in Leviticus includes moral living, not only ritual purity.
uncommon: Israel Knohl argues that the Holiness School wrote after the main priestly source and edited it, widening holiness to all Israel.

sections.b: The Holiness Code repeats "keep my Sabbaths" alongside honoring parents and fearing the sanctuary (19:3, 30; 26:2). Leviticus 23:3 makes the weekly Sabbath the first of the "set times," a "Sabbath of complete rest" wherever Israel lives. Leviticus 25 extends the Sabbath to the land: every seventh year it rests, "a Sabbath for the LORD" (25:2–4). The Day of Atonement is "a Sabbath of complete rest" too (23:32). When Israel refuses, the land will take its Sabbaths in exile (26:34–35, 43).

Leviticus 25 distinguishes two kinds of slavery. An Israelite who grows poor and sells himself must be treated "like a hired worker," not ruled "with crushing cruelty," and freed at the Jubilee, "for they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt" (25:39–43, 55). If sold to a foreigner, his family must buy him back (25:47–54). But slaves bought from the surrounding nations, or from foreigners living in the land, may be kept and passed down "for good" (25:44–46). Defenders of American slavery cited these verses; abolitionists answered with 25:10, "proclaim release," and with the image of God. The tension within the chapter is one of the Bible's sharpest moral questions.

common: The law limited and softened slavery but did not abolish it, and Christians later saw its principles leading beyond it.
uncommon: Some scholars argue that Leviticus 25 was meant to abolish Israelite debt slavery altogether, replacing it with hired labor.

sections.h: The foreigner in the Holiness Code
sections.b: The Holiness Code includes the ger, the foreigner living in Israel, in many of its laws: the blood ban (17:10–13), the sexual laws (18:26), Molech (20:2) and blasphemy (24:16). "You are to have one law for foreigner and native-born alike" (24:22). It also protects him: leave the gleanings "for the poor and for the foreigner" (19:10; 23:22), and "you are to love him as yourself, because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" (19:33–34). Yet Israelites may buy foreigners as permanent slaves (25:45), and God calls Israel itself "foreigners and lodgers" on his land (25:23).

common: Israel's memory of being foreigners in Egypt grounds the command to love the foreigner.

sections.b: Leviticus states the rule in the setting of a court case: "broken bone for broken bone, eye for eye, tooth for tooth. As he put a defect on a person, so it will be put on him" (24:20). It follows the law that whoever kills a person or an animal must make it good (24:17–21), and it ends with "one law for foreigner and native-born alike" (24:22). The word for "defect," mum, is the same used for the defects that bar priests and animals from the altar (21:17–23; 22:20–25). The rabbis ruled that payment is in money (Talmud, Bava Kamma 83b–84a).

Leviticus 26 is the Holiness Code's covenant ending. If Israel walks in God's rules, he will give rain, peace and children, "uphold my covenant with you," and "walk about among you. I will be your God, and you will be my people" (26:3–13). If not, curses come in rising stages, "the revenge of the covenant" (26:25), ending in exile. But God will remember "my covenant with Jacob. Also my covenant with Isaac, and also my covenant with Abraham," and will not break it (26:42–45). The form resembles ancient treaties, such as Esarhaddon's of 672 BC.

The Holiness Code treats the land almost as a living thing. It vomits out nations that defile it (18:24–28; 20:22). It keeps Sabbaths (25:2–7) and will take them by force if refused (26:34–35). It cannot be sold for good, "because the land is mine. You are foreigners and lodgers living with me" (25:23). Families hold their land as tenants of God, and it returns to them at the Jubilee (25:10, 13). When God remembers the covenant with the fathers, he adds, "the land I will remember" (26:42).

Leviticus 23:5–8 places Passover "at twilight" on the fourteenth of the first month, followed by seven days of Unleavened Bread, with holy gatherings on the first and seventh days. The first sheaf of barley is waved during the week (23:9–14). Leviticus gives only the dates; the story and rituals are in Exodus 12.

Leviticus 23:15–21 commands Israel to count seven full weeks from the day the first sheaf was waved, fifty days in all, and then to bring two loaves of the new wheat, baked with leaven, as firstfruits. The count gave the feast its Greek name, Pentecost, "fiftieth." The disputed starting point, "the day after the Sabbath," decided whether the feast could fall on any weekday (the Pharisees) or always on a Sunday (the Sadducees and Karaites). Jewish practice still counts the omer each evening.

Leviticus 23:26–32 repeats the Day of Atonement from the calendar's side: on the tenth of the seventh month the people "humble yourselves," do no work at all, and anyone who does not will be cut off. It is a "Sabbath of complete rest" from evening to evening. The Jubilee is also announced with the ram's horn on this day (25:9), so forgiveness and release begin together.

Leviticus 21–22 sets rules for Aaron's descendants. Priests may mourn only their nearest relatives and must not shave or cut themselves (21:1–6); they marry only Israelite women who are not prostitutes or divorced (21:7). The high priest, anointed and robed, may not mourn even his parents and must marry a virgin of his own people (21:10–15). A priest with a physical defect may not offer at the altar but still eats the holy food (21:16–23). Unclean priests and outsiders may not eat holy things (22:1–16). Jewish kohanim still keep some of these rules.

Leviticus 27:30–33 says that every tithe of grain and fruit is "holy to the LORD" and may be redeemed with a fifth added, and that every tenth animal passing "under the rod" is holy, with no picking good from bad. The rabbis harmonized this with Numbers 18 (for the Levites) and Deuteronomy 14 (eaten at the sanctuary and given to the poor) as several tithes.

Twice Leviticus tells farmers not to harvest to the edge of the field or gather what falls, and not to strip the vineyard bare: "Leave them for the poor and for the foreigner" (19:9–10; 23:22). The Mishnah tractate Peah ("Corner") works this out and sets no fixed minimum, though the rabbis advised at least a sixtieth. Placing the rule inside the festival calendar (23:22) ties the poor to the celebration of harvest.

Leviticus 25 gives the go'el his legal role. When a man grows poor and sells land, "his closest family redeemer is to come and buy back what his brother sold" (25:25). If an Israelite sells himself to a rich foreigner, a brother, uncle, cousin or any close relative may redeem him (25:48–49). The price is set by the years left to the Jubilee. These rules lie behind Boaz's redemption of Elimelech's field (Ruth 4) and Jeremiah's purchase at Anathoth (Jeremiah 32).

Leviticus 18 and 20 list the women a man may not marry or approach: close relatives by blood and by marriage, a woman and her daughter, two sisters at once (18:18), a woman during her period, and a neighbor's wife. These lists became the basis of Jewish and Christian marriage law on forbidden degrees. Henry VIII's case against his first marriage rested on these verses (see the note on Leviticus 20:21). Priests also had special marriage rules (21:7, 13–14).

The Holiness Code guards God's name: do not swear falsely by it (19:12), do not treat it as common (18:21; 22:2, 32), and do not speak it with contempt (24:11, 16). The story of the man who "spoke the Name with contempt" (24:10–23) uses "the Name" alone for God, the usage behind the Jewish HaShem. The refrain "I am the LORD" ends dozens of laws in chapters 18–26.

Leviticus 17–26 calls its laws chuqqot ("rules") and mishpatim ("rulings"), and closes, "These are the rules, the rulings and the laws that the LORD set between himself and the Israelites on Mount Sinai by the hand of Moses" (26:46). "If a human being does them, he will live by them" (18:5) is quoted by Ezekiel, Nehemiah and twice by Paul (Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12). Christian tradition sorted the laws in these chapters into moral, ceremonial and civil kinds, though the chapters themselves mix all three.

sections.b: Leviticus 17 requires every ox, sheep or goat killed by an Israelite to be brought to the tent of meeting as a peace offering, so that none is offered to "goat idols" in the field (17:3–7). Leviticus 22:17–30 sets standards for animals: no defects for vows, at least eight days old, not killed on the same day as their young, and thanksgiving offerings eaten the same day. Leviticus 23 lists the offerings of each feast.

The covenant blessings of Leviticus 26 climb to God's presence: "I will set my dwelling among you, and my soul will not loathe you. I will walk about among you" (26:11–12). The verb is the one used of God walking in Eden (Genesis 3:8). Chapter 24 describes the lamp kept burning "always" and the twelve loaves set before the LORD every Sabbath (24:1–9). Paul quotes 26:12 to call the church "the temple of the living God" (2 Corinthians 6:16).

Leviticus 25:1, 26:46 and 27:34 place the Jubilee, the covenant blessings and curses, and the rules on vows "on Mount Sinai," while the rest of the book is spoken from the tent (1:1). The rabbis asked what the Sabbath year has to do with Sinai and answered that all the commandments, in all their details, were given there (Sifra; Rashi on 25:1).
